title: β-Blocker Ingestion: An Evidence-Based Consensus Guideline for Out-of-Hospital Management
source: Clinical Toxicology, 43:131–146, 2005 (American Association of Poison Control Centers; Wax PM et al.)
about: An evidence-based expert consensus guideline written to assist US poison center personnel in the out-of-hospital triage and initial management of patients with suspected ingestions of β-blockers alone. It reports that in 2003 US poison centers were contacted regarding ingestion of β-blockers by 15,350 patients, 7415 of whom were evaluated in healthcare facilities and 33 of whom died. It reviews current poison center referral practice, therapeutic dose ranges, and the medical literature on toxic doses, time of onset of toxicity, and out-of-hospital treatments, assigning each article a level of evidence. It ends with seven graded recommendations covering referral for self-harm, dose-based referral thresholds (Table 5), activated charcoal, time-since-ingestion windows, ambulance transport, follow-up calls, and observation times for immediate-release, sustained-release and sotalol ingestions. Appendix 4 presents the recommendations as a triage algorithm.

read_for: Abstract: the seven numbered recommendations with their grades (D, C, A, C, D, D, D).

Recommendation 2 / Table 5: refer when the amount exceeds the usual maximum single therapeutic dose or equals the lowest reported toxic dose, whichever is lower (e.g., metoprolol >450 mg IR or >400 mg SR in adults; propranolol >240 mg; sotalol >160 mg; timolol: no safe dose in children).
Recommendation 2: any excess dose taken with a calcium channel blocker, or by a patient with serious underlying cardiovascular disease, warrants referral (Grade C).
Recommendation 3: do not induce emesis; consider oral activated charcoal but do not delay transportation to give it (Grade A).

Recommendation 4: asymptomatic patients over the referral dose go to an emergency department if the ingestion was within 6 hours (immediate-release other than sotalol), 8 hours (sustained-release) or 12 hours (sotalol) of the call (Grade C).

Recommendation 7: observe asymptomatic referred patients at least 6 hours (IR), 8 hours (SR) or 12 hours (sotalol); routine 24-hour admission after an unintentional sustained-release ingestion is not warranted (Grade D).
Recommendation 1: stated or suspected self-harm or malicious administration is referred immediately regardless of dose (Grade D).
Appendix 2: Grades of Recommendation A–D and Z mapped to levels of evidence 1a–6 (case series and single case reports are level 4, Grade C; expert opinion is level 5, Grade D).

Background and Definitions: β-blockers decrease cyclic AMP production and blunt catecholamine effects; propranolol's high lipid solubility raises the likelihood of seizures; sotalol also antagonizes the potassium channel; acute exposure is defined as no more than 8 hours.
Conclusions, Specific Pharmacological Therapy: in-hospital literature supports intravenous glucagon, but no studies address its out-of-hospital use.

Limitations of the Published Data: dose-history uncertainty, lack of analytical confirmation and unverified ingestion times.

terms.chapter_definition: Drugs that antagonize the β-adrenergic receptor; they competitively block β-adrenergic receptors resulting in decreased cyclic AMP production and a blunting of catecholamine effects.
An exposure occurring over a period of no more than 8 hours.
An exposure that occurs over a period of 8 or more hours.
For the purpose of this guideline, 1) children under 6 years of age and 2) older children and adults.

Ingestion of an amount that exceeds the usual maximum single therapeutic dose or an amount equal to or greater than the lowest reported toxic dose (whichever is lower) warrants consideration of referral to an emergency department.
Any sign, symptom, or laboratory/electrocardiographic finding consistent with β-blocker toxicity.
If the actual dose ingested cannot be ascertained, the amount of the drug product that is missing from the container is multiplied by the concentration of the formulation.

terms.term: Level of evidence / Grade of recommendation
terms.chapter_definition: Articles were assigned level-of-evidence scores from 1 to 6 based on the Grades of Recommendation table developed by the Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine at Oxford University; single case reports were classified along with case series as level 4 (Grade C), expert opinion is level 5 (Grade D).
A nonselective β-adrenergic antagonist that is particularly toxic because it also antagonizes the potassium channel; it carries a 12-hour referral window and observation period.
The Toxic Exposure Surveillance System of the American Association of Poison Control Centers, the source of the 2003 exposure and fatality counts.
